tldr: Focusing on the theoretical robustness guarantees of policy regularisation, this paper proposes SMM-AC, a novel extension to continuous control, demonstrating that regularisation substantially improves sim-to-real transfer and robustness to real-world perturbations.
hero_caption: Sim-to-real robustness evaluation on physical robots. Top: In the Franka arm lifting task with an off-center cube, unregularised baselines like PPO and FastTD3 fail to grasp, whereas regularised methods like SAC and SMM-AC reliably succeed. Bottom: On ANYmal-D stair climbing under observation noise, unregularised methods stumble and fail, while regularised methods successfully complete the traversal.
overview:
When applying reinforcement learning to robotics, sim-to-real transfer—training in simulation and deploying to physical hardware—is widely used. In practice, however, weakly regularised algorithms like PPO remain the default choice. The practical benefits of policy regularisation for real-world transfer have remained poorly characterised.

To address this, the authors focus on the theoretical duality between regularised reinforcement learning and robust reinforcement learning. Introducing regularisation should implicitly provide robustness against unforeseen environmental shifts and perturbations. To test this hypothesis, they extend the Soft MellowMax (SMM) value function—known for its provably large robustness guarantees—to continuous control, developing a novel actor-critic algorithm called SMM-AC.

In addition to MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks, the authors evaluate their approach on two real robotic platforms: a Franka manipulator arm and an ANYmal-D quadruped. SMM-AC matches strong baselines like SAC in simulation while achieving the highest returns on physical hardware.

Furthermore, across various real-world perturbations—including observation noise, shifts in mass and center of mass, reduced friction on wet surfaces, and added payloads—SMM-AC minimizes performance degradation and displays superior robustness. Regularisation does not simply replace domain randomisation; rather, combining both dramatically improves real-world deployability.
contributions: Extending the discrete-action Soft MellowMax (SMM) value function to continuous control, deriving and proposing the practical off-policy algorithm SMM-AC.
Demonstrating on MuJoCo benchmarks that SMM-AC achieves high sample efficiency and average return competitive with standard continuous control baselines such as SAC and TD3.

Proving on two real robots (a Franka arm and ANYmal-D) that regularised RL, particularly SMM-AC, achieves superior sim-to-real transfer and perturbation robustness over unregularised methods like PPO.
Showing that regularised methods maintain physical deployability even when domain randomisation (DR) ranges are narrowed, establishing that regularisation and DR complement each other.

sections.heading: Why regularised RL for sim-to-real, and why now?
sections.summary: While PPO remains the de facto standard in sim-to-real robotics pipelines, robustness against unknown dynamics shifts and real-world perturbations is still a major hurdle. This section introduces the theoretical robustness guarantees of regularised RL, motivating the derivation of SMM-AC for continuous control.
sections.details:
In robot learning, sim-to-real transfer—training policies in simulation before deploying them on real robots—is the dominant paradigm. Weakly regularised, on-policy algorithms like PPO have long served as the default workhorse. Recently, scaling off-policy RL on massively parallel simulators has enabled direct transfer to quadrupeds and humanoids. However, most prior studies have focused solely on nominal task performance under identical training conditions.

Real-world deployment inevitably introduces sensor noise, environmental shifts, and robot dynamics discrepancies that cannot be fully captured in simulation—the well-known sim-to-real gap. The standard defense is domain randomisation (DR), but DR requires engineers to specify perturbation parameters in advance.

In contrast, regularised RL—which adds a policy regularisation penalty—possesses a mathematical duality with robust RL, implicitly conferring robustness against worst-case adversarial perturbations. If these theoretical guarantees hold in practice, regularised policies should be inherently resilient to unforeseen disturbances.

This study focuses on Soft MellowMax (SMM), which theoretically induces a larger robust set than standard entropy regularisation. While SMM was previously restricted to discrete-action Q-learning, the authors extend it to continuous control via an actor-critic method, SMM-AC, and thoroughly evaluate its transfer capabilities on real manipulators and quadrupeds.

captions.F1: Overview of physical robot robustness experiments. Top: Franka lifting an off-center cube unseen during training. Bottom: ANYmal-D climbing stairs under observation noise. In both cases, regularised methods demonstrate superior resilience.

sections.heading: The link between regularisation, robustness, and SMM
sections.summary: A review of regularised Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) and the theoretical foundations explaining why regularisation confers robustness. The section also positions entropy-regularised methods like SAC alongside the broader robustness guarantees of the Soft MellowMax value function.
sections.details:
In regularised MDPs, a strongly convex regularisation term $\Omega(\pi)$ is added to the objective to penalize extreme or undesirable policy distributions. For example, using negative entropy encourages the action distribution toward uniformity, which forms the core principle of Soft Actor-Critic (SAC).

Prior work has shown that regularised RL not only smooths the optimization landscape to stabilize training, but also mathematically guarantees that policies maintain return under worst-case dynamics and reward perturbations. Essentially, a larger robust set—governed by the regulariser and temperature parameters—allows a policy to withstand broader environmental variations.

This leads to Soft MellowMax (SMM). In discrete action spaces, SMM was proposed as an alternative soft maximization operator to log-sum-exp (which corresponds to entropy regularisation). Recent theoretical work proves that SMM-based RL induces a strictly larger robust set than entropy regularisation.

However, in continuous action spaces, evaluating SMM requires integrating over a reference policy—a softmax distribution over Q-values—which cannot be solved analytically. This intractable denominator has historically prevented SMM from being used in continuous robotic control.

sections.heading: Bridging to continuous control: SMM-AC with three networks
sections.summary: To address the intractable reference policy of SMM in continuous domains, SMM-AC introduces a slowly updated reference network alongside the standard actor and critic. This design preserves SAC-like stability while guiding exploration toward sharper, high-return regions.
sections.details:
Under SMM, the policy is regularised via KL divergence to remain close to a reference policy $\pi^{\text{ref}}$, which is defined as a softmax distribution over Q-values. While SAC encourages uniform random exploration, SMM explores around regions deemed promising by the current Q-function. It serves as an intermediate approach, combining SAC's ability to discover diverse trajectories with PPO's pull toward high-return regions.

In continuous spaces, computing the partition function in the reference policy's denominator is intractable. To resolve this, the authors introduce an architecture trained with three neural networks:

### Critic Learning
The critic $Q_\theta$ is updated to minimize temporal difference error using a one-sample Monte Carlo estimate of the regularised value function, following the standard SAC design.

### Actor Learning
The actor $\pi^{\text{act}}_z$ is trained to match the optimal softmax policy. Optimizing directly against raw critic outputs caused severe training instability. To address this, the reference network is used as a low-variance surrogate, shielding the actor from critic noise and ensuring stable gradient updates.

### Introducing the Reference Network
This is the core architectural contribution. The reference policy $\pi^{\text{ref}}_\phi$ is maintained as an independent network and updated using an SAC-like loss at a much smaller learning rate than the actor. This slow update provides a stable anchor, enabling seamless continuous-action optimization.

Because this setup reuses standard SAC replay buffers and network architectures, it integrates easily into modern high-throughput off-policy frameworks such as FlashSAC.

sections.heading: Simulation benchmarks: Evaluating performance on MuJoCo
sections.summary: On standard continuous control MuJoCo benchmarks, SMM-AC demonstrates competitive sample efficiency and return compared to SAC, TD3, and PPO. Matching or exceeding SAC across nearly all tasks confirms its effectiveness as a general continuous control algorithm.
sections.details:
To establish baseline performance, the authors compared SMM-AC against SAC, TD3, and PPO across standard MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks (Ant, HalfCheetah, Hopper, Humanoid, Pusher, Swimmer, Walker2d, etc.) using CleanRL implementations.

In SMM-AC, the reference inverse temperature was fixed to $\alpha=1$, while the policy inverse temperature $\omega$ was swept. Aside from a mid-training performance collapse in InvertedDoublePendulum, SMM-AC achieved learning speeds and asymptotic returns on par with strong baselines like SAC and TD3.

The appendix also evaluates FlashSMM-AC, an implementation within the GPU-accelerated FlashSAC framework. Here, FlashSMM-AC matched FlashSAC and outperformed FastTD3 and PPO.

A key takeaway is that SMM-AC does not necessarily crush SAC in nominal simulation scores alone. Rather, its primary advantage emerges during real-world transfer under perturbations, as explored in the robotic experiments.

captions.F2: Training curves (episode return vs. environment steps) on MuJoCo benchmark environments. SMM-AC (solid teal) achieves high returns and convergence speeds competitive with SAC (solid black) across most tasks, with the exception of InvertedDoublePendulum.

sections.heading: Robotic experiments: Regularisation beats gaps and perturbations
sections.summary: Sim-to-real transfer was tested across four tasks on a Franka arm and an ANYmal-D quadruped. SMM-AC not only attained higher returns than baselines on hardware, but also exhibited minimal performance loss under sensor noise, mass variations, and slippery surfaces.
sections.details:
The core of the paper evaluates sim-to-real transfer across four robotic environments: a Franka Panda manipulator (Reach to target, Lift cube) and an ANYmal-D quadruped (flat ground and rough terrain velocity tracking).

### 5.1 Experimental Setup and Injected Perturbations
Baselines included PPO, FastTD3, and SAC, evaluated against SMM-AC. For hardware safety, policies with simulation failure rates over 80% under perturbations were barred from physical deployment. Consequently, PPO and FastTD3 were excluded from all ANYmal perturbation tests.
Physical robots were subjected to severe real-world perturbations:
- Observation Noise: Gaussian noise added to Franka joint/end-effector readings; noise added to ANYmal proprioceptive inputs ($\sigma=0.001$).
- Physical Parameter Changes: Franka lifting a cube with double mass or a 15 mm shifted center of mass.
- Environmental Changes: ANYmal walking on wet concrete (low friction), carrying a 7 kg torso payload, and receiving manual lateral pushes on flat terrain.

### 5.2 Sim-to-Real Transfer Performance (Nominal)
In unperturbed settings (the 'none' row in Table 2), regularised methods (SAC, SMM-AC) substantially outperformed PPO and FastTD3 on ANYmal locomotion, particularly on rough terrain. On Franka Lift, SMM-AC achieved the highest score with significantly lower variance across seeds than SAC or PPO, demonstrating reliable deployment.

### 5.3 Post-Deployment Perturbation Robustness
Evaluating both absolute return and performance retention (percentage of nominal return preserved) under perturbations highlighted SMM-AC's distinct advantage:
- Resistance to Observation Noise: While observation noise degraded all methods, PPO failed completely and SAC suffered heavy performance drops. SMM-AC maintained significantly higher returns.
- Physical and Environmental Perturbations: On Franka, SMM-AC retained nearly 100% of its performance with heavy or off-center cubes, where baselines failed. On ANYmal, SMM-AC maintained noticeably higher returns under low friction and the 7 kg payload compared to SAC.

These results confirm that the theoretical robust set induced by regularisation functions as an effective real-world safety margin against severe operational disturbances.

sections.heading: Conclusions and future directions
sections.summary: Through SMM-AC and extensive hardware trials, the authors demonstrate that regularised RL bridges the sim-to-real gap and boosts real-world perturbation robustness. Furthermore, regularisation acts as a natural complement to domain randomisation rather than a replacement.
sections.details:
This study derives SMM-AC, bringing the theoretical robustness guarantees of the Soft MellowMax value function into continuous control by introducing a slowly updated reference network.

Following simulation validation, real-world deployment on a Franka arm and ANYmal-D proved that regularised RL—especially SMM-AC—delivers superior transfer performance and disturbance resistance over unregularised methods like PPO and FastTD3. The algorithm showed remarkable resilience against everyday disturbances such as sensor noise, shifted object mass distributions, and sudden friction drops.

Experiments progressively reducing domain randomisation (DR) showed that while narrower DR degrades all policies, regularised methods remain deployable in regimes where unregularised policies fail completely. Regularisation is not a silver bullet that eliminates the need for DR; instead, pairing both provides complementary synergy that raises real-world deployment reliability.

A key avenue for future work is developing an autotuning schedule for the inverse temperature $\omega$, as optimal values currently vary across tasks.

sections.heading: Appendix: DR reduction experiments and implementation details
sections.summary: The appendix details experiments on progressively reducing domain randomisation (DR), presents the formal derivation of the SMM-AC loss function, and provides hyperparameters used in the FlashSAC implementation.
sections.details:
The appendix provides supplementary mathematical derivations and extended experimental evaluations supporting the main claims.

### Detailed Domain Randomisation (DR) Reduction Experiments
Policies were trained across three shrinking levels of DR in both simulation and reality: Level 1 (standard), Level 2 (narrowed), and Level 3 (nearly fixed nominal dynamics). On ANYmal, this involved narrowing friction ranges, removing base pushes, and eliminating initial pose variations.
As DR decreased, returns dropped across all algorithms. Under DR 3, no model met the hardware safety criterion (failure rate below 80%) on flat terrain. However, under intermediate DR 2, regularised methods like SMM-AC remained functional while PPO and FastTD3 failed, with SMM-AC maintaining the highest return across all DR levels.

### Loss Derivation and High-Speed Implementation
The actor loss derivation eliminates the action-independent partition function and applies the reparameterisation trick to construct a low-variance expectation estimator. In FlashSMM-AC (built on FlashSAC for GPU-parallel simulation), training remained remarkably stable even at higher inverse temperature ranges ($\omega=100 \sim 400$) than those used in CleanRL.

takeaways: While PPO is conventionally favored in sim-to-real pipelines, regularised RL algorithms (SAC and SMM-AC) substantially boost hardware transfer rates and disturbance robustness.
The theoretical robustness guarantees of regularised RL translate directly into real-world benefits, enhancing resilience against sensor noise, mass variations, and friction drops.
Regularisation and domain randomisation (DR) are complementary rather than mutually exclusive; combining them maximizes the success rate of real-world deployment.
In continuous action spaces, anchoring SMM with a slowly updated reference network prevents actor divergence and ensures stable optimization.
limitations: The optimal inverse temperature parameter ($\omega$) varies significantly depending on the task and reward scale, and SMM-AC currently lacks an automatic temperature tuning mechanism like SAC.
Some task instabilities persist, such as mid-training performance collapse observed in MuJoCo's InvertedDoublePendulum environment.
Maintaining and updating an additional reference network increases model complexity and expands the hyperparameter tuning space.
